sources: BirdLife International, Seabird of the month: Atlantic Puffin (2022): average about 10 fish per trip, British record 62 fish at once; dives as deep as 40 m and stays under up to a minute; uses its wings underwater so it looks like it is flying under water; digs burrows in the ground or between rocks; bright orange bills and feet in breeding season fade to duller shades in winter; lives over 20 years, oldest recorded 36; https://www.birdlife.org/news/2022/04/06/seabird-of-the-month-atlantic-puffin-fratercula-arctica

BBC Countryfile, How do puffins manage to catch so many fish in one go?: a modified tongue and a series of spines on the upper palate; the tongue pushes each fish against the spines so it can catch more; https://www.countryfile.com/wildlife/birds/how-much-fish-puffins-carry

University of Nottingham press release (2019), Puffin bills 'glow' under UV light: Jamie Dunning found by accident that the bill ridges of a dead puffin fluoresce under UV light; https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/news/pressreleases/2019/jan/puffin-bills-%27glow%27-under-uv-light-study-discovers.aspx

Smithsonian Magazine (2019), Scientists film a puffin scratching its back with a stick (Fayet et al., PNAS, Oxford): a camera trap on Grimsey Island, Iceland filmed an Atlantic puffin pick up a stick and scratch itself, the first documented tool use in a seabird; https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/first-scientists-film-puffin-scratching-its-back-stick-180973883/

beats.say: This bird can cram sixty-two fish into its beak at once.
So I shrank myself down to fish size, to see how it does it.
The Atlantic puffin. A tuxedo body, and a clown-colored beak.
Its tongue pins each fish against spikes on the roof of its mouth.
So it can open its beak again, and grab another, and another.
To hunt, it flaps its wings underwater, like it's flying through the sea.
It can dive as deep as forty meters, and stay under for a whole minute.
On land, it digs a burrow in the ground, or between the rocks.
That bright orange beak is only for the breeding season. In winter, it fades.
And under ultraviolet light, parts of its beak glow.
A scientist found that by accident, shining a UV lamp on a dead puffin.
Some live over twenty years. The oldest known was thirty-six.
But the strangest part? One was caught on camera using a tool.
It picked up a stick, and scratched itself with it.
The first time a seabird was ever seen using a tool.
Could you fit sixty-two fish in your mouth?
A bird with a fish buffet in its face, and its own back scratcher.
Follow me. Next, a fish that walks out of the water.
